title: The race (Hebrews 12:1–2)
hookLine: run with endurance, looking to Jesus

cards: Late in a marathon. The crowd has thinned. The legs are lead.
On this stretch the race stops being about speed and becomes about not stopping. Then someone on the curb shouts your name, and somehow you take the next step.
An early Christian letter takes a scene like that, the long race and the crowd, and turns it into a picture of the life of faith. It doesn't promise a sprint. It promises a crowd.

teach.b: Hebrews, chapter twelve, in the King James words: "Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us."
Start with the cloud of witnesses. The chapter before is a long roll call: Abel, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Moses, Rahab and more, people who trusted God without seeing the end.

Now the writer gathers them around the runners like a cloud. Some readers picture them in the stands, watching; others hear witnesses as people whose lives bear witness. Either way, the runners aren't alone.
Then, lay aside every weight. Nobody runs a long race in a winter coat. Some weights are sins.
Some are just heavy: old grudges, worry, the need to look good.

Then, run with patience. The Greek word here, hupomone, has more grit than the English: endurance, staying power, the strength to keep moving when it's hard. Yesterday's patience was a farmer waiting.
Today's is a runner who won't quit.

Then the turn: "Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame." Eyes up. Not on your feet, not on the runner next to you.
On the one who has already finished. Something waiting at the finish, the writer says, was worth the course.

how: Some churches read Hebrews 12 at funerals and on All Saints' Day, remembering those who have gone before as a cloud of witnesses, and the image of the race appears in sermons, hymns and prayers for perseverance.

o: a sprint to finish good works before the end comes
a contest where believers compete to be the holiest
the life of faith as a long run, with a crowd of witnesses

games.q: you're running the long race of Hebrews 12, and you're tired. where does the letter tell you to look?
o: unto Jesus, the author and finisher of your faith.
at the runner just ahead of you.
games.why: looking unto Jesus, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross. the eyes go to the one who already finished.

practice: Think of one long race you're in right now, a hard job, an illness, a marriage in a rough season, a habit you're trying to break, caring for someone, and notice one weight in it you could set down, even for today.

Then picture your own cloud of witnesses in the stands: one or two people, living or gone, who ran something hard before you. If you pray, you can look to Jesus with the letter's words, the author and finisher of our faith.

wordCard.voice: The race. In Hebrews, the life of faith as a long run: a cloud of witnesses in the stands, every weight laid aside, and eyes on Jesus at the finish.

orig.note: Greek: endurance, steadfastness — the word the King James renders "patience" in Hebrews 12:1.

carryVoice: Your line: run with patience. Nobody on this track runs it alone. I'll be here tomorrow.
